_comment: Question bank for the Complexity Quiz (site/pages/lc-complexity-quiz.html).
Each entry shows a Python snippet and asks for its time and space complexity.
id         unique slug; the quiz keys its per-question state off it
lc         LeetCode number, or null for a pure algorithm / Python drill
title      required only when lc is null — otherwise README.md supplies it
difficulty required only when lc is null — otherwise README.md supplies it
topic      the bucket shown in the score breakdown and the topic filter
vars       what each symbol in the answer means; shown above the inputs
note       the ground rule for this question (what counts as space, etc.)
code       the snippet, one array element per line
accept     other answers graded correct — for genuinely debatable ones only
why        the explanation shown after answering
trap       the wrong answer people actually give, and why it is wrong
site/build-quiz.js validates every entry (unique id, README-known lc, parseable
answers) and fails the build rather than shipping a question nobody can score.

questions.why: One pass, and every dict lookup and insert is O(1) on average. The dict can end up holding all n values.
questions.trap: `target - x in seen` is a hash lookup, not a scan — it does not make the loop quadratic. That is what separates this from the brute-force O(n^2) version.

questions.why: One pass over the prices, carrying two scalars. Nothing grows with the input.

questions.title: Iterative binary search
questions.why: The search window halves every iteration, so it survives log2(n) rounds. Three integers is the whole state.

questions.title: Recursive binary search — with slicing
questions.why: `nums[:mid]` copies the half it keeps. The copies cost n/2 + n/4 + ... = O(n), which swamps the log n comparisons; the live slices cost O(n) memory too.
questions.trap: This looks like textbook O(log n) / O(1) binary search. Passing `lo`/`hi` indices instead of slices is what actually gets you there — this is the single most common way a correct algorithm loses its complexity in Python.

questions.note: Ignore the space held by the result list.
code: while lo < hi and nums[lo] == nums[lo + 1]:
questions.why: The outer loop is n and each two-pointer sweep is O(n), so O(n^2) — which dominates the O(n log n) sort. Space is whatever the sort needs: Timsort is O(n), an in-place sort would be O(log n), and the pointers themselves are O(1).
questions.trap: The nested `while lo < hi` inside the `else` looks like a third level of nesting, but `lo` and `hi` only ever move toward each other, so the whole inner block is one linear sweep.

code: if not stack or stack.pop() != pairs[ch]:
questions.why: Each character is pushed and popped at most once. An all-opening string like "((((" puts every character on the stack.
Pointers are rewired in place — three references, whatever the list length.
questions.trap: The equally common recursive version is O(n) space: it puts one stack frame per node.

questions.why: Once both pointers are inside the cycle, the gap closes by one node per step, so they meet within n steps. Two pointers is the entire state.
questions.trap: The `seen = set()` solution is the same O(n) time but O(n) space — Floyd's tortoise and hare is what buys you the constant space.

questions.vars: n, m = lengths of the two lists
questions.why: Every node is visited once and spliced in place — no new nodes are allocated, only the dummy head.
Kadane's algorithm is a one-dimensional DP whose table has been collapsed to a single rolling value.
questions.trap: Writing the loop as `for x in nums[1:]` would quietly make it O(n) space — the slice copies the array.

questions.vars: n = len(s), k = size of the character set
code: if ch in seen and seen[ch] >= left:
questions.why: `right` advances once per character and `left` never moves backwards, so it is one pass. The dict holds one entry per distinct character — bounded by the alphabet, and by n in the worst case.
questions.trap: This window never re-scans: `left` jumps straight past the duplicate rather than walking. The naive shrink-one-at-a-time variant is still O(n) amortised, but the version that restarts the scan is O(n^2).

code: if 0 <= i < m and 0 <= j < n and grid[i][j] == "1":
questions.why: Each cell is sunk at most once, so the total DFS work is linear in the number of cells. Space is the recursion stack, and a snake-shaped island makes it as deep as the grid is large.
questions.trap: Answering O(1) space because the grid is modified in place misses the call stack — the usual follow-up is "what if the grid is 10^6 cells?", which is asking for the iterative BFS.

code: q = deque((i, j) for i in range(m) for j in range(n) if grid[i][j] == 2)
fresh = sum(row.count(1) for row in grid)
if 0 <= x < m and 0 <= y < n and grid[x][y] == 1:
questions.why: Multi-source BFS enqueues each cell at most once and does O(1) work per cell. The queue can hold most of the grid when everything rots at the same time.
questions.trap: The `for _ in range(len(q))` inner loop is the level marker, not extra work — it partitions the same O(m*n) dequeues into rounds.

code: q = deque(c for c in range(numCourses) if indeg[c] == 0)
questions.why: Kahn's algorithm dequeues each node once and walks each edge once. The adjacency list is O(V + E); the in-degree array and queue are O(V).
questions.trap: The nested `for nxt in graph[c]` is not a second factor of V — summed over all nodes it visits each edge exactly once, which is the E term.

questions.vars: n = number of nodes, h = tree height
questions.why: Every node is visited once. The stack holds one frame per level of the current path — O(log n) for a balanced tree, O(n) for a skewed one, so O(h) either way.
questions.trap: "O(log n) space" is only true if the tree is balanced, and the problem never promises that. Say O(h) and then say what h is in the worst case.

code: level = [kid for node in level for kid in (node.left, node.right) if kid]
questions.why: Each node lands in exactly one level list. The widest level of a balanced tree holds about n/2 nodes, so the frontier alone is O(n).

questions.vars: n = len(nums), k = the k asked for
code: return [val for cnt, val in heap]
questions.why: Counting is O(n); the heap is capped at k, so each of the (at most n) pushes costs log k. Space is dominated by the Counter, which can hold n distinct values.
questions.trap: Capping the heap at k is the whole point — `heapq.nlargest(k, freq)` is the same idea. Pushing everything first would be O(n log n).

questions.vars: n = total nodes across all lists, k = len(lists)
code: heap = [(node.val, i, node) for i, node in enumerate(lists) if node]
questions.why: Every node is pushed and popped once, and the heap never holds more than one node per list, so each operation is log k.
questions.trap: Merging the lists pairwise down the array instead is O(n * k) — the heap is what turns the k factor into log k.

questions.vars: n = len(nums), k = the k asked for
questions.why: A min-heap of size k: n pushes at log k each, and the heap holds exactly k elements once it fills.
questions.trap: Quickselect does the same job in O(n) average time and O(1) space — that is the follow-up this question is fishing for.

questions.note: Count the recursion and scratch state only — the `res` list is the output.
questions.why: There are n! permutations and copying each one out costs n, so O(n * n!). Auxiliary space is just the recursion stack, n frames deep, because the swaps mutate `nums` in place.
questions.trap: O(n!) time undercounts: producing a permutation is not free, the `nums[:]` copy is O(n).

questions.note: Here the output counts — `res` is the only thing that grows.
questions.why: The result doubles on every one of the n iterations, giving 2^n subsets. Building each one costs its length, and the subsets average n/2 elements — so both the work and the memory are O(n * 2^n).
questions.trap: O(2^n) counts the subsets but not their contents. Any answer that enumerates variable-length outputs needs the length factor.

code: return -1 if dp[amount] == float("inf") else dp[amount]
questions.why: One table cell per amount, each filled by trying all n coins. The table is the only storage.
questions.trap: This is pseudo-polynomial: `a` is the *value* of the input, not its length, so doubling the number of digits in `amount` squares the work. Interviewers like to push on that.

questions.why: The DP array has been rolled down to the two values the recurrence actually reads.
questions.trap: Treating the big-integer additions as O(1) is the usual simplification, and it is the answer an interviewer wants — but the numbers do grow to n bits.

questions.why: Each call branches in two and the recursion tree is roughly n deep, so about 2^n nodes (tightly, phi^n). But only one root-to-leaf path is live at a time, so the stack is n frames.
questions.trap: Answering O(2^n) space confuses the size of the recursion tree with the depth of the stack. The tree is explored depth-first — the calls do not coexist.

code: prev, cur = cur, max(cur, prev + x)
questions.why: One pass, and the recurrence only ever looks two cells back — so two variables replace the table.

questions.vars: m, n = the two string lengths
questions.why: Every cell of the (m+1) x (n+1) table is filled once with O(1) work.
questions.trap: Space drops to O(n) if you keep only the previous row — worth saying out loud, since each cell reads only the row above and the cell to its left.

questions.why: The inner loop runs 0 + 1 + ... + (n-1) = n(n-1)/2 times, which is O(n^2). One DP entry per index.
questions.trap: `for j in range(i)` shrinking to nothing at i=0 does not save an order — the triangular sum is still quadratic.

questions.why: One binary search per element over a list that never exceeds n entries. `tails` holds the smallest possible tail for each subsequence length.
questions.trap: `tails` is not the increasing subsequence — only its length is meaningful. The complexity question and the correctness question both hinge on that.

questions.why: Still one unit of work per grid cell, but only one row is ever stored — each cell needs the value above it (the old `row[j]`) and the one to its left (the already-updated `row[j-1]`).
questions.trap: O(m * n) space is right for the two-dimensional table, not for this rolling one. Spotting that the table collapses to a row is exactly what the follow-up asks for.

questions.why: The two pointers close on each other, so the loop runs n times total, carrying four scalars.
questions.trap: The prefix/suffix-max array version is the same O(n) time but O(n) space. The two-pointer trick is precisely what removes the arrays.

questions.why: Amortised: every index is pushed exactly once and popped at most once, so the inner `while` does at most n pops across the whole run.
questions.trap: A loop inside a loop is not automatically O(n^2). This is the monotonic-stack argument — count total pushes and pops, not the shape of the nesting.

questions.vars: n = items currently on the stack
questions.note: Time is for a single push / pop / getMin call.
code: cur_min = min(val, self.stack[-1][1]) if self.stack else val
questions.why: Each entry carries the minimum of everything below it, so getMin is a peek. The price is a second value stored per element.
questions.trap: `min(...)` here compares two values, not the whole stack — reading it as a scan is what makes people answer O(n).

questions.note: Time is for a single get / put call.
questions.why: OrderedDict is a hash map over a doubly linked list, so `move_to_end` and `popitem(last=False)` are pointer surgery, not a re-sort. The map never exceeds the capacity.
questions.trap: `move_to_end` sounds like it shifts elements. It relinks one node — this is the whole reason the hash-map-plus-linked-list design is the expected answer.

questions.note: Time is for a single insert / search call.
questions.why: One dict hop per character, independent of how many words the trie already holds — that independence is the whole reason to build one. A fresh insert adds at most L nodes.
questions.trap: Search does not depend on the number of stored words, so no `n` belongs in either answer.

questions.vars: n = number of nodes (the matrix is n x n)
code: if isConnected[i][j] and j not in seen:
questions.why: Each node is visited once, and visiting it scans its whole matrix row — n rows of n entries. Space is the `seen` set plus a recursion stack that is at most n deep.
questions.trap: This is the O(V + E) DFS bound in disguise: an adjacency *matrix* makes E = n^2 whether or not the edges exist.

code: for u, v, w in times:
return max(dist.values()) if len(dist) == n else -1
questions.why: Lazy Dijkstra pushes once per edge, so the heap holds up to E entries and each operation is log E, which is O(log V) for a simple graph. Space is the adjacency list plus the heap.
questions.trap: The `if u in dist: continue` line is what makes this correct without a decrease-key: stale heap entries are allowed in and skipped on the way out.

questions.why: The extra branching decides *which* half to keep; it still throws one half away each iteration.
questions.trap: With duplicates allowed (LC 81) the `nums[lo] <= nums[mid]` test stops distinguishing the halves and the worst case degrades to O(n).

code: return sum((p + speed - 1) // speed for p in piles)
questions.why: Binary search on the *answer*: log m candidate speeds, and checking one costs a full O(n) pass over the piles. The generator in `sum` does not materialise a list.
questions.trap: The log factor is over the value range, not the array length — the two are unrelated, and mixing them up is the classic slip on binary-search-on-answer problems.

questions.vars: n = len(strs), k = length of the longest word
questions.why: Sorting each word is k log k, done n times. Every word plus its key is stored, so the map holds O(n * k) characters.
questions.trap: The k factor is easy to drop. Counting characters into a 26-tuple key instead makes it O(n * k) time — a real improvement worth naming.

questions.why: Two sorts dominate the linear comparison, and `sorted` builds two new lists of n characters.
questions.trap: A one-liner is not automatically O(n). `sorted` on a string returns a list — both the sort and that list are real costs. `Counter(s) == Counter(t)` is the O(n) alternative.

questions.note: The returned list is the output; do not count it as auxiliary space.
questions.why: Two sequential passes, not nested ones. The prefix products are staged inside the output array and the suffix product is carried in a single variable — no second array.
questions.trap: Two loops in a row add, they do not multiply: O(n) + O(n) is O(n).

questions.vars: m, n = the two filled lengths
questions.why: Filling from the back means nothing is ever shifted: each of the m + n values is written exactly once, in place.
questions.trap: Merging forwards would need either a copy (O(m + n) space) or a shift per insert (O(m * n) time). Writing backwards is what buys both.

questions.why: XOR is associative and self-cancelling, so the pairs annihilate and the loner survives — in one accumulator.
questions.trap: The set-based solution is O(n) space. This problem is asked precisely to see whether you find the O(1)-space one.

questions.vars: n = the integer, b = its bit width (32 here)
questions.why: `n &= n - 1` clears the lowest set bit, so the loop runs once per set bit — at most 32 for a fixed-width integer, which is a constant. Stated in the input's bit width it is O(b), and b = log n.
questions.trap: Calling it O(n) treats the *value* as the input size. For a fixed 32-bit word every bit trick is O(1); the honest general answer is O(b) over the word width.

code: for lo, hi in ((i, i), (i, i + 1)):
while lo >= 0 and hi < len(s) and s[lo] == s[hi]:
questions.why: n centres, each expanding up to n characters. The only storage is `best`, a slice of up to n characters — track indices instead and it becomes O(1).
questions.trap: The two-entry tuple loop is a constant factor (odd and even centres), not a third n.

questions.vars: n = len(points), k = the k asked for
code: heapq.heappush(heap, (-(x * x + y * y), x, y))
return [[x, y] for _, x, y in heap]
questions.why: A bounded max-heap of the k best so far: n pushes at log k each, k entries held.
questions.trap: Sorting all the points is O(n log n) — worse whenever k is much smaller than n, which is the case the problem is built around.

questions.why: The sort dominates the single linear merge pass. Space is the output list plus Timsort's scratch — both O(n).
questions.trap: Almost every interval problem is O(n log n) for exactly this reason: the sort, not the sweep, sets the bound.

questions.why: Sort is n log n; then n heap operations at log n each — same order. The heap holds one end time per concurrent room, up to n.
questions.trap: `rooms[0]` is the earliest ending meeting, a peek at the heap root: O(1), not a scan.

code: while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
questions.why: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n): log n levels of merging, O(n) work per level. Each level of the recursion holds O(n) of copied slices, and the stack is only log n deep.
questions.trap: Unlike a recursive binary search that slices, the copying here does not change the order — merge sort already does O(n) work per level, so the slices are free in Big-O terms.

questions.vars: m, n = board dimensions, L = len(word)
code: if not (0 <= i < m and 0 <= j < n) or board[i][j] != word[k]:
found = (dfs(i + 1, j, k + 1) or dfs(i - 1, j, k + 1)
or dfs(i, j + 1, k + 1) or dfs(i, j - 1, k + 1))
return any(dfs(i, j, 0) for i in range(m) for j in range(n))
questions.why: Every cell can start a search, and each search branches four ways at each of L characters. Space is the recursion stack, L frames deep — the board is marked in place and restored.
questions.trap: 3^L is the tighter bound (you never walk straight back into the cell you came from), but 4^L is the answer usually expected. Either way the exponent is the *word* length, not the board size.

questions.note: Time is for a single addNum call.
questions.why: A bounded number of heap pushes and pops per call, each log n. Every number added is kept in one of the two heaps.
questions.trap: The three heap operations are a constant factor, not a multiplier. And `findMedian` is O(1) — it only peeks at the two roots.

questions.why: The same amortised monotonic-stack argument: n pushes, at most n pops, O(1) work each. The stack can hold every index when the bars are strictly increasing.
questions.trap: Being a Hard problem does not make it superlinear. The brute force is O(n^2); the stack is what removes the second factor.

questions.why: The `if x - 1 not in s` guard means the inner walk only starts at a run's first element, so every value is walked exactly once across the whole loop.
questions.trap: The nested `while` reads as O(n^2), and it would be without that guard. Drop the guard and each element of a long run re-walks the run.

questions.why: One pass, one dict lookup per element. The dict holds up to n distinct prefix sums.
questions.trap: The counter must hold *how many times* each prefix sum occurred, not just whether it occurred — but that does not change either bound.

code: if not best or right - left < len(best):
questions.why: `right` and `left` each traverse s once, so the window is linear despite the inner loop. Space is the counter (one entry per distinct character of t) plus `best`, which can be up to n characters.
questions.trap: The `while need[s[left]] < 0` loop never rewinds `left`, so it is amortised O(n) over the whole run — not O(n) per outer step.

questions.title: Building a string with +=
questions.why: Python strings are immutable, so `out += ch` allocates a new string and copies the old one: 1 + 2 + ... + n character copies. `"".join(chars)` is the O(n) version.
questions.trap: CPython has an in-place optimisation that can make this look linear when the string has one reference, but it is an implementation detail with no guarantee — the answer to give in an interview is O(n^2), plus the join.

questions.title: `in` on a list, inside a loop
questions.why: `x in b` on a list is a linear scan, so the one-line body hides an m-step loop.
questions.trap: The same `in` on a set or dict is O(1). `b = set(b)` before the loop turns this into O(n + m) time for O(m) space — the single highest-value one-line fix in Python interviews.

questions.title: Draining a list with pop(0)
questions.why: `list.pop(0)` shifts every remaining element down one slot, so it is O(n) per call and O(n^2) over the drain.
questions.trap: This is why BFS uses `collections.deque`: `popleft()` is O(1), while the same code on a list quietly makes the traversal quadratic. `list.pop()` from the end *is* O(1).

questions.title: heapify, then pop k times
questions.vars: n = len(nums), k = how many to take
questions.why: `heapify` is O(n) — bottom-up sift-down, not n insertions — and each of the k pops is log n. The output list holds k items; the heap is `nums` itself, in place.
questions.trap: Calling heapify O(n log n) is the classic overcount. The nodes near the leaves, which are most of them, sift down almost no distance, and the series sums to O(n).

questions.title: Nested loop starting at i + 1
questions.why: The inner loop runs n-1, n-2, ..., 1 times: n(n-1)/2 iterations, which is O(n^2).
questions.trap: "It only does half the work" is true and irrelevant — halving is a constant factor. Big-O does not see it.

questions.title: Loop whose work halves each round
questions.why: n + n/2 + n/4 + ... < 2n. A geometric series with ratio 1/2 converges, so the whole thing is linear.
questions.trap: O(n log n) is the reflex: log n rounds times "a loop". But the loop shrinks — only the *first* round costs n, and everything after it adds up to less than one more n.

questions.title: Loop with a doubling counter
questions.why: i takes the values 1, 2, 4, 8, ... so it reaches n after log2(n) steps.
questions.trap: Any loop whose variable is *multiplied* rather than incremented is logarithmic — the mirror image of the halving binary search.

questions.title: Sorting inside a loop
questions.why: n iterations, and iteration i slices (O(i)) then sorts (O(i log i)) — summing to O(n^2 log n). Only one window is alive at a time, so space is O(n).
questions.trap: A `sorted()` call inside a loop is never free. The two-heap MedianFinder does this same job in O(log n) per element.
